_note: Coordinates use the current IAU standard (positive-east longitude). Landing sites use the Davies & Colvin (1987/2000) precise values. Crew names, eponyms, and historical detail cross-referenced against NASA and Wikipedia sources.

landmarks.name: Apollo 11
landmarks.note: Tranquility Base, July 20, 1969. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked the surface while Michael Collins orbited alone in the Command Module — the first crewed Moon landing.

landmarks.name: Apollo 12
landmarks.note: November 1969. Charles "Pete" Conrad and Alan Bean made a precision landing close enough to walk to the robotic Surveyor 3 probe and retrieve parts from it; Richard Gordon orbited above.

landmarks.name: Apollo 14
landmarks.note: February 1971, Fra Mauro highlands. Alan Shepard — America's first man in space, a decade earlier — and Edgar Mitchell walked here; Shepard famously hit two golf balls before departing. Stuart Roosa orbited.

landmarks.name: Apollo 15
landmarks.note: July 1971, Hadley–Apennine. David Scott and James Irwin were the first to drive the Lunar Roving Vehicle here; Al Worden orbited, at one point the most isolated human being in history.

landmarks.name: Apollo 16
landmarks.note: April 1972, Descartes Highlands. John Young and Charles Duke walked here — Young later commanded the first Space Shuttle flight in 1981. Ken Mattingly orbited.

landmarks.name: Apollo 17
landmarks.note: December 1972, Taurus–Littrow — the last crewed Moon landing. Eugene Cernan, the last person to step off the surface, walked with Harrison "Jack" Schmitt, a trained geologist and the only professional scientist to walk on the Moon.

landmarks.name: Tycho
landmarks.note: Named for Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish astronomer whose exceptionally precise naked-eye observations gave Kepler the data to derive the laws of planetary motion. The crater's ray system, radiating over a thousand kilometers, is only about 108 million years old — young by lunar standards.

landmarks.name: Copernicus
landmarks.note: Named for Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543), who proposed the heliocentric model placing the Sun at the center of the solar system. Nicknamed the 'Monarch of the Moon' for its sharply terraced rim and central peaks.

landmarks.name: Aristarchus
landmarks.note: Named for Aristarchus of Samos (c. 310–230 BC), who proposed a Sun-centered solar system some 1,800 years before Copernicus. The crater is the brightest large feature on the Moon, visible even by earthshine.

landmarks.name: Plato
landmarks.note: Named for the Greek philosopher Plato (c. 428–348 BC). Its lava-flooded floor is notably smooth and dark, unlike the rugged terrain around it.

landmarks.name: Kepler
landmarks.note: Named for Johannes Kepler (1571–1630), who formulated the three laws of planetary motion using Tycho Brahe's observations. A young, bright crater with an extensive ray system.

landmarks.name: Grimaldi
landmarks.note: Named for Francesco Maria Grimaldi (1618–1663), the Italian Jesuit scientist who discovered the diffraction of light and helped produce an influential early telescopic map of the Moon. One of the darkest features on the lunar surface.

landmarks.name: Aristoteles
landmarks.note: Named for the Greek philosopher Aristotle (384–322 BC), who used the Moon's curved shadow during lunar eclipses as evidence the Earth is round.

landmarks.name: Aristillus
landmarks.note: Named for Aristyllus (fl. c. 280 BC), an early Greek astronomer working in Alexandria who, with Timocharis, compiled one of the first true star catalogs using numerical position measurements.

landmarks.name: Montes Apenninus
landmarks.note: The Moon's grandest mountain range, its peaks rising up to 5 km — debris thrown up by the same ancient impact that formed Mare Imbrium. Apollo 15 landed at its base.

landmarks.name: Rima Hadley
landmarks.note: A sinuous canyon, likely a collapsed lava tube, that David Scott and James Irwin drove alongside in the Lunar Roving Vehicle during Apollo 15, sampling its rim for the mission's geology team.

landmarks.name: Mare Imbrium
landmarks.note: The 'Sea of Rains' — the Moon's largest and most dominant nearside basin, formed by an asteroid impact roughly 3.9 billion years ago and later flooded with dark basaltic lava.

landmarks.name: Mare Serenitatis
landmarks.note: The 'Sea of Serenity,' bordered by the Apennine and Caucasus mountains, connecting southeastward to Mare Tranquillitatis.

landmarks.name: Mare Crisium
landmarks.note: The 'Sea of Crises' — a strikingly round, isolated dark patch near the eastern limb, filled with lava after an ancient asteroid impact.

landmarks.name: Mare Tranquillitatis
landmarks.note: The 'Sea of Tranquility,' named in 1651 by astronomers Grimaldi and Riccioli — over three centuries before Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin gave it its lasting fame.

landmarks.name: Oceanus Procellarum
landmarks.note: The 'Ocean of Storms' — the only lunar plain large enough to earn the name 'Oceanus,' covering over 10% of the Moon's total surface area.

landmarks.name: Sinus Iridum
landmarks.note: The 'Bay of Rainbows' — a semicircular bay opening onto Mare Imbrium, ringed by the Jura mountains. When sunlight catches the peaks while the bay floor is still dark, it forms the striking effect known as the 'Golden Handle.'
